title: asd
description: Android SDK Downloader — a dependency-free, pure-Dart CLI that fetches Android SDK components from the Myket mirror, bypassing sdkmanager.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
`asd` (Android SDK Downloader) is a single-file, dependency-free Dart CLI that downloads Android SDK components (platforms, build-tools, NDK, etc.) directly from the [Myket](https://myket.ir) mirror (`maven.myket.ir`), as a drop-in alternative to Google's `sdkmanager`.

It's a pure-Dart rewrite: no `aria2c`, `curl`, `unzip`, or `awk` subprocesses. HTTP requests, SHA-1 checksums, and ZIP extraction are all implemented directly against `dart:io`, `dart:convert`, and `dart:typed_data`. The whole tool lives in one file: `bin/asd.dart`.

## Why

`sdkmanager` can be slow or unreliable depending on your network/region. `asd` points at the Myket mirror instead and adds resumable, multi-connection downloads, automatic checksum verification, and self-healing installs (`--fix`) — all without shelling out to external programs.

## 1. Install

Two ways to get the `asd` binary onto your machine — see [Installation](/asd/installation/) for details:

- **Offline installer (recommended)** — a single self-contained executable with `asd` embedded inside it.
- **Manual** — download the `asd` binary directly from Releases.

## 2. Fetch the package registry

Before anything else, `asd` needs its package registry (a CSV file listing every available SDK component, version, download URL, and checksum):

```bash
asd --update
```

This downloads the registry from `https://maven.myket.ir/sdk-archives.csv`, filters it down to Linux packages only, and caches it locally (default: `~/.cache/asd/myket.csv`).

## 3. Install something

```bash
asd platform-tools
asd ndk
asd build-tools 34.0.0
```

See [Commands](/asd/commands/) for the full command reference and [Configuration](/asd/configuration/) for environment variables.

## Requirements

- Dart SDK `>=3.0.0 <4.0.0` (only needed to *build* `asd` — the compiled binary has no runtime dependency on Dart).
- Linux or Windows. (The registry `asd --update` fetches is filtered to Linux packages; the tool itself also builds and runs on Windows.)
Getting Started.Installation:
`asd` ships as native, dependency-free executables built by CI on every push, published as [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/myket-com/asd/releases) tagged `v<pubspec-version>.r<run-number>`.

## Offline installer (recommended)

The installer is a single executable with the `asd` binary embedded inside it (base64-encoded at build time). Running it just writes `asd` to disk — nothing is downloaded, there's no second file to keep track of.

1. Download `installer-linux` (or `installer-windows.exe`) from [Releases](https://github.com/myket-com/asd/releases).
2. Run it:

```bash
chmod +x installer-linux
./installer-linux                 # installs to /usr/local/bin, re-execs with sudo if needed
./installer-linux ~/.local/bin    # or a directory you already own — no sudo required
```

On Windows, run `installer-windows.exe`. It defaults to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\asd\bin`.

If the target directory isn't already on your `PATH`, the installer prints the exact line to add (`export PATH="<dir>:$PATH"` on Linux, `setx PATH "%PATH%;<dir>"` on Windows).

## Manual

Download `asd-linux` (or `asd-windows.exe`) from [Releases](https://github.com/myket-com/asd/releases), rename it to `asd` (or `asd.exe`), and place it anywhere on your `PATH`.

## After installing

Fetch the package registry once before first use:

```bash
asd --update
```

## Building from source

```bash
dart pub get
dart compile exe bin/asd.dart -o asd

# the installer needs the asd binary fused into it first
dart run tool/embed_installer.dart asd bin/installer.dart installer_embedded.dart
dart compile exe installer_embedded.dart -o installer
```

`bin/installer.dart` ships with a placeholder (`__ASD_BASE64_PLACEHOLDER__`) in place of the real payload, so compiling it directly produces an installer that refuses to run with a clear error message. `tool/embed_installer.dart` reads the compiled `asd` binary, base64-encodes it, and substitutes it into a throwaway copy of `installer.dart` before *that* gets compiled. See [Architecture](/asd/architecture/) for how the embedding step works internally.

Arch Linux users building locally will already have `dart` available via the AUR (`dart-sdk` or similar) or the official Dart tarball; there's no distro package required at runtime since the compiled binary is fully self-contained.
Getting Started.Configuration:
`asd` is configured entirely through environment variables — there's no config file.

| Variable | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ANDROID_HOME` | `~/dev/Android/Sdk` | Android SDK root directory. Every installed component is placed under here, mirroring the same path layout `sdkmanager` uses (e.g. `ndk/27.0.12077973`, `build-tools/34.0.0`). |
| `ASD_CSV` | `~/.cache/asd/myket.csv` | Path to the local CSV package registry fetched by `asd --update`. |
| `ASD_CONNECTIONS` | `16` | Max parallel HTTP connections used for multi-connection (ranged) downloads. Automatically scaled down for small files — see [Downloads](/asd/downloads/). |
| `ASD_SKIP_CHECKSUM` | unset | Set to `1` to always skip SHA-1 checksum verification, even when the registry has one on file. |

`HOME` (or `USERPROFILE` on Windows) is read to resolve the defaults above; if neither is set, `asd` falls back to the current directory (`.`).

## Avoiding sudo

`asd` will transparently re-launch itself with `sudo` if it hits a permission error while writing to `ANDROID_HOME` or `ASD_CSV` (see [Sudo Handling](/asd/sudo-handling/)). To sidestep that entirely, point both variables at directories you already own:

```bash
export ASD_CSV=~/.local/share/asd/myket.csv
export ANDROID_HOME=~/.local/share/android-sdk
asd --update
```

Add these exports to your shell profile (`~/.bashrc`, `~/.zshrc`, etc.) to make them permanent.

Guides.Commands:
`asd` takes a single subcommand (or a package name) plus optional arguments:

```
asd <command> [args]
```

| Command | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `asd <name> [version]` | Download and install an SDK component. `version` defaults to the latest available. |
| `asd --list, -l [name]` | List available packages in the registry, optionally filtered by name. |
| `asd --installed, -i [name]` | List installed SDK components, optionally filtered by name. |
| `asd --remove, -rm <name>` | Remove an installed SDK component. |
| `asd --fix, -f [name]` | Check and repair broken, corrupted, or orphaned packages. |
| `asd --update, -up` | Refresh the local package registry from the Myket mirror. |
| `asd --verify, -v <name> [version]` | Verify the checksum of an installed component (skipped automatically if the registry has no checksum for it). |
| `asd --help, -h` | Show usage help. |

Running `asd` with no arguments is equivalent to `--help`.

## Examples

```bash
asd ndk                         # install latest NDK
asd ndk 27.0.12077973           # install a specific NDK version
asd build-tools 37.0.0-rc2      # install a specific build-tools version
asd -l ndk                      # list all NDK versions in the registry
asd -l                          # list every package in the registry
asd -i                          # list all installed components
asd -i ndk                      # list installed NDK components only
asd -rm ndk                     # remove installed NDK
asd -f ndk                      # fix a broken NDK installation
asd -up                         # refresh the package registry
asd -v ndk 27.0.12077973        # verify checksum of an installed NDK version
```

## Package identifiers

Packages are addressed by the same semicolon-separated path segments the Android SDK registry itself uses internally, e.g. `build-tools;34.0.0` or `ndk;27.0.12077973`. When you run `asd ndk 27.0.12077973`, it's matched against a registry row whose path is either exactly `ndk;27.0.12077973`, or whose path equals `ndk` with a matching version column — see `findMatch` in [Architecture](/asd/architecture/) for the exact matching rules.

## Unknown flags

Any argument starting with `-` that isn't a recognized flag is rejected immediately with `Unknown option '<flag>'` rather than being treated as a package name — so `asd --lsit` fails fast instead of silently trying to install a package literally named `--lsit`.
Guides.Downloads: caching, resume, and speed:
Archives are downloaded into a `downloads/` folder next to the CSV registry (e.g. `~/.cache/asd/downloads/`) instead of a throwaway temp directory. That single design choice is what makes resume, `--fix`, and `--verify` all work without re-fetching data unnecessarily.

## Resume after failure

If a download is interrupted — network error, Ctrl-C, power loss — the next attempt at the same package picks up where it left off instead of restarting from zero. This applies both to:

- **Single-connection downloads**, via an HTTP `Range` request starting at the byte count already on disk.
- **Multi-connection (ranged) downloads**, where each chunk file (`<name>.zip.part0`, `.part1`, ...) independently resumes from its own last byte.

If the server doesn't honor the `Range` header (responds `200` instead of `206`), `asd` detects this and restarts that transfer from zero rather than corrupting the file.

## Multi-connection downloads

For files larger than 4 MiB, `asd` splits the download into up to `ASD_CONNECTIONS` (default `16`) parallel ranged requests, each writing to its own `.partN` file, then concatenates them once all chunks finish. The number of connections actually used is auto-scaled down for small files (never more than `ceil(totalSize / 4MiB)` connections) so tiny packages don't spin up 16 requests for a 500 KB file.

Each chunk retries and resumes **independently** on error — up to 5 attempts per chunk, with exponential backoff (`500ms * attempt`) — instead of failing the whole download because one connection hiccuped.

If the server doesn't advertise `Accept-Ranges: bytes`, or the file size is unknown or below the threshold, `asd` falls back to a single resumable connection automatically.

## Live progress

While downloading, `asd` prints percentage, bytes downloaded/total, current transfer speed, and an ETA, refreshed several times a second (throttled to avoid flooding the terminal):

```
Downloading... 42.3% (128.4MB / 303.9MB) 18.2MB/s ETA 00:09
```

Speed is sampled over a rolling ~400ms window rather than an all-time average, so the ETA reacts to real network conditions rather than smoothing them away.

## Reuse across commands

Because successfully downloaded archives stay cached in `downloads/` rather than being deleted after extraction... actually they *are* deleted after a successful install to save space, but a cached archive from a **previous** verify or a partially-completed install can still be reused by `--fix` and `--verify` without re-downloading, since both check for an existing cached ZIP with a matching name before fetching again.
Guides.Repairing Installations:
Two commands exist for keeping an SDK installation trustworthy over time: `--fix` for structural repair, and `--verify` for cryptographic verification against the registry.

## `asd --fix`

`asd --fix` (or `-f`) walks every `package.xml` under `ANDROID_HOME` and, for each installed package, checks:

1. The `package.xml` is present and parseable (has a readable `path`, `display-name`, and revision).
2. The package still exists in the current registry — packages removed upstream are **reported and skipped**, not blindly reinstalled.
3. The install directory actually contains files (not just an empty shell).
4. If a cached archive from a previous download still exists locally, its SHA-1 checksum still matches the registry entry.

Anything broken (empty directory, unreadable `package.xml`, or a checksum mismatch on the cached archive) is wiped and reinstalled automatically. Anything merely *orphaned* (no longer present in the registry) is reported without being touched, since `asd` has no way to safely reinstall a package it no longer knows about.

```bash
asd --fix              # check and repair everything installed
asd --fix ndk          # check and repair only packages matching "ndk"
```

Running `--fix` with no matches prints `All packages OK.`; otherwise it summarizes how many were fixed, failed, or skipped.

## `asd --verify`

`asd --verify <name> [version]` re-downloads the archive for an *already-installed* component and compares its SHA-1 against the registry's checksum column, printing both values:

```bash
asd --verify ndk 27.0.12077973
```

```
Registry checksum:   1a2b3c...
Downloaded checksum: 1a2b3c...
Checksum OK. Archive is authentic.
```

If the registry has no checksum on file for that package, `--verify` says so and exits without downloading anything — there's nothing to check it against.

## Skipping checksum verification

Set `ASD_SKIP_CHECKSUM=1` to bypass checksum checks everywhere they'd normally happen (fresh installs, `--fix`, and the checksum step of `--verify` itself is unaffected since you asked for it explicitly, but `--fix`'s *diagnosis* step will skip flagging cached-archive mismatches). Useful on flaky mirrors where checksums occasionally don't match due to upstream inconsistencies you've already decided to trust.
Guides.Sudo Handling:
`asd` never assumes it needs root, and it never asks you to prefix every command with `sudo` manually.

## How it works

Every operation is attempted as the current user first. Only if the OS reports a permission error (`FileSystemException` with errno `13`/`EACCES`, `1`/`EPERM`, or `5`/`EIO`, depending on platform) does `asd` transparently re-launch itself with `sudo`, passing through the exact same arguments and inheriting your terminal (`ProcessStartMode.inheritStdio`) so the password prompt still works normally.

This retry-with-sudo behavior only applies on **Linux and macOS**. On Windows, a permission error just prints a message telling you to re-run the command from an elevated (Administrator) terminal — there's no Windows equivalent of transparent re-exec.

To prevent infinite re-exec loops, the re-launched process sets `ASD_SUDO_REEXEC=1` in its environment; if a permission error still occurs *after* that, `asd` gives up and reports the error normally instead of retrying again.

If `sudo` itself isn't installed or the user declines/fails authentication, `asd` reports `sudo is not available or was denied.` and exits with a non-zero status.

## Avoiding sudo entirely

The need for `sudo` almost always comes from `ANDROID_HOME` (default `~/dev/Android/Sdk`) or `ASD_CSV` (default `~/.cache/asd/myket.csv`) pointing at a location your user doesn't own — which is uncommon for the defaults, but common if you've pointed `ANDROID_HOME` at a system-wide SDK install shared by other tools.

Point both at directories you already own to sidestep sudo entirely:

```bash
export ASD_CSV=~/.local/share/asd/myket.csv
export ANDROID_HOME=~/.local/share/android-sdk
asd --update
```

See [Configuration](/asd/configuration/) for the full list of environment variables.
Guides.Executable Permissions:
SDK archives — NDK toolchains, `emulator`, `platform-tools`, and others — ship files that must remain executable after extraction, and in some cases contain symlinks (e.g. `libc++.so` pointing at a versioned file). Naively extracting a ZIP with `dart:io`'s stock decoder loses both of these, since standard ZIP inflation only cares about file contents.

## How `asd` preserves them

`asd` implements ZIP extraction itself (see [Architecture](/asd/architecture/)) specifically so it can read the extra metadata Info-ZIP/`zip`/`ditto`-style archives store in each central directory entry's **external attributes** field:

- The high 16 bits of the external attributes, when the archive's "version made by" host OS byte indicates Unix, encode a standard Unix file mode (permission bits + file type).
- A mode whose file-type bits equal `0xA000` marks the entry as a symlink; its "file content" is the link target path as plain text rather than real file data.

During extraction, `asd`:

1. Detects symlink entries and recreates them with `Link.create(target)` instead of writing file bytes — skipped on Windows, where symlinks require elevated privileges to create and aren't meaningful for Android SDK tooling anyway.
2. For regular files, extracts the permission bits (`mode & 0x1FF`) and applies them with `chmod` after writing the file.

This means `asd`-installed tools — `aapt`, NDK's `clang`, `emulator`'s launcher scripts, etc. — are executable immediately, with no manual `chmod +x` step required after install.

This section documents its internal structure for anyone building on, forking, or auditing the tool. None of this is a published Dart package API (there's no `lib/` — `asd` is an application, not a library), but the file is organized into clearly delimited sections that map to the pages below.

## Design principles

- **Zero dependencies.** `pubspec.yaml` declares no `dependencies:` at all — only an `environment: sdk` constraint. Every capability (HTTP client, ZIP inflate, SHA-1) that a typical project would pull in via `pub` is implemented directly against the standard library.
- **Single file.** The entire tool is `bin/asd.dart`. This is a deliberate trade-off: easy to audit end-to-end and trivially portable (copy one file), at the cost of it being long.
- **Fail loud, fail typed.** Expected failure modes throw `AsdException`, caught once in `main` and printed as `Error: <message>` with exit code `1`. Unexpected `FileSystemException`s get special handling for the sudo-retry path (see [Sudo Handling](/asd/sudo-handling/)).
API Reference.CSV Registry:
## `PkgEntry`

```dart
class PkgEntry {
  final String path;      // e.g. "ndk;27.0.12077973"
  final String name;      // display name, e.g. "NDK (Side by side)"
  final String rev;       // version string, e.g. "27.0.12077973"
  final String url;       // download URL for the archive
  final String checksum;  // SHA-1 hex, or empty if the registry has none
}
```

One `PkgEntry` is built from one CSV row on demand — the registry isn't parsed into a `List<PkgEntry>` up front; `readCsvRows` returns raw `List<List<String>>` rows, and `findMatch` builds a single `PkgEntry` only for the row that matches.

## `readCsvRows`

Reads `ASD_CSV`, skips the header row, drops blank lines, and splits each remaining line on `,`. Throws `AsdException` if the file doesn't exist yet (telling the user to run `asd --update` first) or can't be read.

## `findMatch`

```dart
PkgEntry? findMatch(List<List<String>> rows, String name, String version)
```

Matching logic, in order:

- If `version` is given: match a row whose path column is exactly `<name>;<version>`, **or** whose path equals `name` and whose version column (`row[2]`) equals `version`. This dual check exists because some registry rows use a semicolon-joined path for the version and others put the version in its own column.
- If `version` is empty: match the **first** row whose path equals `name` exactly, or starts with `<name>;` — i.e. the first (typically latest, given registry ordering) available version.

Returns `null` if nothing matches, which callers turn into an `AsdException` naming the requested package and version.

## `ensureCsvAvailable`

A small guard called at the top of every command that needs the registry (`doInstall`, `doRemove`, `doFix`, `doVerify`): if `ASD_CSV` doesn't exist yet, it transparently runs `doUpdate` first rather than failing, so a fresh install doesn't require the user to remember to run `--update` manually before their first real command.

## `doUpdate`

Fetches `https://maven.myket.ir/sdk-archives.csv` over plain HTTP GET, then filters out any line whose lowercase form contains `windows`, `macos`, or `darwin` — keeping the header row plus Linux-only entries — before writing the result to `ASD_CSV`. This filtering is why the registry is meaningfully smaller than Google's full `sdkmanager` package list.
API Reference.HTTP & Download Engine:
## `downloadFile`

```dart
Future<void> downloadFile(String url, String destPath)
```

The public entry point for all downloads. It first issues a `HEAD` request to learn the content length and whether the server supports `Accept-Ranges: bytes`, then picks a strategy:

- **Ranged, multi-connection** (`_downloadRanged`) — used when the file is larger than `_minChunkSize` (4 MiB), the server advertises range support, and more than one connection would actually be used given the file size.
- **Single, resumable** (`_downloadSingleResumable`) — the fallback for everything else (small files, unknown size, or a server that doesn't support ranges).

The `HEAD` request itself is wrapped in a `try/catch` — if it fails outright (some mirrors reject `HEAD`), `asd` just falls back to a single connection with unknown total size rather than aborting.

## `_downloadSingleResumable`

Reads the current on-disk file size (if any) and, if the server supports ranges, requests `bytes=<offset>-` to continue where it left off. If the server responds `200` instead of the expected `206` for a ranged request, `asd` detects the mismatch and restarts the write from byte zero rather than corrupting the file with misaligned data. Retries up to `_maxChunkRetries` (5) times with a linear backoff of `500ms * attempt`.

## `_downloadRanged` / `_downloadChunkToFile`

Splits `[0, totalSize)` into `connections` roughly-equal byte ranges, each downloaded to its own `<destPath>.partN` file. Each chunk:

- Resumes independently from its own current `.partN` size if one already exists on disk (from a previous interrupted attempt).
- Retries independently up to 5 times with the same backoff as the single-connection path.

Once every chunk finishes, the parts are concatenated in order into the final file and the `.partN` files are deleted.

## `_Progress`

Tracks bytes received against a rolling ~400ms sampling window to compute current speed, throttles terminal repaints to roughly every 150ms, and renders either a percentage+ETA line (when total size is known) or a running byte count (when it isn't). Speed and size are formatted with `_humanSize`/`_humanDuration` helpers (binary units: B/KB/MB/GB, `1024` divisor).
API Reference.package.xml Handling:
`asd` tracks installed components the same way `sdkmanager` does: a `package.xml` file inside each install directory, in the same schema Android Studio's SDK Manager expects, so `asd`-installed packages are recognized by other Android tooling without translation.

## `PkgXmlInfo` and `parsePackageXml`

```dart
class PkgXmlInfo {
  final String path;     // e.g. "ndk;27.0.12077973"
  final String name;     // display name
  final String version;  // "major.minor.micro"
}
```

Parsing is done with targeted regular expressions rather than a full XML parser — again, in service of the zero-dependency constraint — extracting `<localPackage path="...">`, `<display-name>`, and `<major>`/`<minor>`/`<micro>`. Returns `null` (rather than throwing) if the file can't be read or the `path` attribute is missing, which callers treat as "this doesn't look like a valid package.xml."

## `writePackageXml`

Splits a revision string like `27.0.12077973` on `.` into major/minor/micro (defaulting missing segments to `0`) and writes a minimal but schema-compatible `package.xml`:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<ns2:repository xmlns:ns2="http://schemas.android.com/repository/android/common/02">
    <localPackage path="ndk;27.0.12077973">
        <revision>
            <major>27</major>
            <minor>0</minor>
            <micro>12077973</micro>
        </revision>
        <display-name>NDK (Side by side)</display-name>
    </localPackage>
</ns2:repository>
```

Written once, right after successful extraction, at the end of `doInstall`.

## `countNonXmlFiles`

Recursively counts files under a directory that *aren't* named `package.xml`. Used by `--fix`'s diagnosis pass to distinguish a genuinely empty/broken install (0 content files, `package.xml` written but extraction silently failed or was interrupted) from a healthy one.
API Reference.Commands:
Implementation notes for each subcommand, beyond what's covered in the [Guides](/asd/guides/) section.

## `doInstall`

The full install pipeline: resolve the package via `findMatch`, compute the destination path from the package's semicolon-joined path segments under `ANDROID_HOME`, download the archive into the `downloads/` cache (see [Downloads](/asd/downloads/)), verify its checksum (unless `ASD_SKIP_CHECKSUM=1` or the registry has none), extract it, flatten a single wrapping subdirectory if present, write `package.xml`, and delete the cached ZIP on success. Any failure at any stage throws `AsdException` and leaves the cached archive in place so a retry can resume the download rather than starting over.

## `doRemove`

Finds every registry path matching the given name (exact or semicolon-prefixed, so `asd -rm ndk` removes *every* installed NDK version, not just one), deletes each corresponding directory recursively, and throws if none of the matched paths were actually installed.

## `doFix`

Two modes depending on whether a name filter is given:

- **No filter:** walks `ANDROID_HOME` recursively for every `package.xml`, diagnoses each installed package (see `_diagnosePackage` below), and repairs anything broken.
- **With a filter:** finds the first `package.xml` whose path contains the filter string, diagnoses just that one, and repairs it if needed — or reports `is OK.` if not.

### `_diagnosePackage`

Returns one of five `_PkgIssue` values by checking, in order: is `package.xml` parseable → does the install directory have any non-XML files → does the package still exist in the current registry → (if a cached archive exists) does its SHA-1 still match. The first failing check wins; later checks aren't run once an issue is found.

### `_repairPackage`

Deletes the broken directory entirely and calls `doInstall` again with the same path/version recovered from the old `package.xml` — repair is always a clean reinstall, never a partial patch.

## `doVerify`

Looks up the package in the registry, confirms it's actually installed, and — if the registry has a checksum on file — re-downloads the archive (reusing the `downloads/` cache if a matching file is already there) purely to recompute and compare its SHA-1. This is a **read-only sanity check**: it never touches the installed files themselves, only the cached/re-downloaded archive.

## `doList` / `doInstalled`

Both produce the same three-column, sorted, deduplicated (`Set<String>`) output format (`PACKAGE`, `NAME`, `VERSION`) via the shared `formatRow` helper — `doList` reads from the registry CSV, `doInstalled` reads from `package.xml` files actually found on disk under `ANDROID_HOME`.

## Project layout

```
asd/
├── bin/
│   ├── asd.dart          # the entire tool
│   └── installer.dart    # offline installer (payload injected at build time)
├── tool/
│   └── embed_installer.dart  # injects the base64 asd binary into installer.dart
├── pubspec.yaml
├── README.md
└── LICENSE
```

There is no `lib/` directory — `asd` is distributed purely as compiled executables, not as a Dart package other projects import.
Project.Build & Release Process:
## Local build

```bash
dart pub get
dart compile exe bin/asd.dart -o asd

dart run tool/embed_installer.dart asd bin/installer.dart installer_embedded.dart
dart compile exe installer_embedded.dart -o installer
```

`tool/embed_installer.dart` is a standalone Dart script (not part of the shipped tool) that:

1. Reads the compiled `asd` binary as raw bytes and base64-encodes it.
2. Reads `bin/installer.dart`'s source and replaces the literal placeholder string `__ASD_BASE64_PLACEHOLDER__` with that base64 payload.
3. Writes the result to a new source file (`installer_embedded.dart`), leaving the original `installer.dart` untouched.

That generated source is then compiled normally with `dart compile exe`. The result is a single, fully self-contained `installer` executable with `asd` baked directly into its binary — nothing is fetched at install time, and there's no separate `asd` file to lose track of alongside the installer.

If you compile `bin/installer.dart` directly without running the embed step first, the placeholder is still present, and the installer detects this at runtime and refuses to run with a clear error pointing at this build step instead of silently writing a corrupt binary.

## CI

Every push builds `asd` and `installer` for both Linux and Windows and publishes all four artifacts (`asd-linux`, `asd-windows.exe`, `installer-linux`, `installer-windows.exe`) as a GitHub Release, tagged `v<pubspec version>.r<run_number>` — combining the version declared in `pubspec.yaml` with the CI run number, so every CI run produces a uniquely tagged release even between version bumps.
Project.FAQ:
### Why not just use `sdkmanager`?

`sdkmanager` works fine for most people. `asd` exists for cases where Google's servers are slow, rate-limited, or blocked for a given network/region — it points at the [Myket](https://myket.ir) mirror instead, and adds resumable multi-connection downloads and self-healing repair on top.

### Does `asd` require Java or Android Studio?

No. `asd` is a standalone compiled binary with no runtime dependency on Java, Android Studio, or Dart itself — only the Dart SDK is needed to *build* it from source.

### Is the installed layout compatible with Android Studio / Gradle?

Yes — `asd` writes the same `package.xml` schema `sdkmanager` uses, under the same semicolon-path directory layout (e.g. `$ANDROID_HOME/ndk/27.0.12077973`), so other Android tooling recognizes `asd`-installed components without any translation step.

### Why does `asd` sometimes ask for my sudo password?

Only if `ANDROID_HOME` or `ASD_CSV` point at a location your user doesn't own (system-wide paths, for instance). See [Sudo Handling](/asd/sudo-handling/) for exactly when this triggers, and [Configuration](/asd/configuration/) for how to avoid it by pointing both variables at directories you already own.

### Can I use `asd` on macOS?

The tool's Dart source is largely platform-agnostic (sudo re-exec explicitly supports macOS, for instance), but CI currently only builds and publishes binaries for Linux and Windows. Building from source on macOS with `dart compile exe` should work, but is unverified/untested by the project.

### What happens if a download is interrupted halfway through?

Nothing is lost — see [Downloads: caching, resume, and speed](/asd/downloads/). The next attempt at installing the same package resumes from the exact byte offset it left off at, for both single- and multi-connection downloads.

### Where does the package registry come from?

`https://maven.myket.ir/sdk-archives.csv`, fetched by `asd --update` and filtered down to Linux-only entries before being cached locally at `ASD_CSV`.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
`asd` (Android SDK Downloader) is a single-file, dependency-free Dart CLI that downloads Android SDK components directly from the [Myket](https://myket.ir) mirror (`maven.myket.ir`), as an alternative to Google's `sdkmanager`.

This is the **2.0.0** release. Compared to 1.0.0, this version adds an offline, self-contained installer: `asd`'s compiled binary is base64-embedded directly into the `installer` executable at build time, so a single file can install `asd` with nothing else to download or keep track of. See [Installation](/asd/2.0.0/installation/) for details.

## 1. Install

See [Installation](/asd/2.0.0/installation/) for the offline installer (recommended) or manual download.

## 2. Fetch the package registry

```bash
asd --update
```

Downloads the registry CSV from `https://maven.myket.ir/sdk-archives.csv`, filters it to Linux packages, and caches it locally (default: `~/.cache/asd/myket.csv`).

## 3. Install something

```bash
asd platform-tools
asd ndk
asd build-tools 34.0.0
```

See [Commands](/asd/2.0.0/commands/) for the full command reference and [Configuration](/asd/2.0.0/configuration/) for environment variables.

## Requirements

- Dart SDK `>=3.0.0 <4.0.0` (only needed to *build* `asd`).
- Linux or Windows.
Getting Started.Installation:
`asd` 2.0.0 ships as native executables built by CI, published as GitHub Releases. This version introduces the **embedded offline installer**, replacing 1.0.0's two-file installer.

## Offline installer (recommended)

The installer has the `asd` binary base64-embedded directly inside its own executable at build time. Running it writes `asd` to disk — nothing else is fetched, and there's no second file to keep alongside it (unlike 1.0.0, where the installer needed `asd` sitting next to it in the same directory).

```bash
chmod +x installer-linux
./installer-linux                 # installs to /usr/local/bin, re-execs with sudo if needed
./installer-linux ~/.local/bin    # or a directory you already own — no sudo required
```

On Windows, run `installer-windows.exe` (defaults to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\asd\bin`).

## Manual

Download `asd-linux` (or `asd-windows.exe`) from Releases, rename it to `asd`, and place it on your `PATH`.

## Building from source

```bash
dart pub get
dart compile exe bin/asd.dart -o asd

dart run tool/embed_installer.dart asd bin/installer.dart installer_embedded.dart
dart compile exe installer_embedded.dart -o installer
```

`tool/embed_installer.dart` is new in 2.0.0: it reads the compiled `asd` binary, base64-encodes it, and substitutes it into a throwaway copy of `installer.dart` (replacing the placeholder `__ASD_BASE64_PLACEHOLDER__`) before that copy is compiled. Compiling `bin/installer.dart` directly, without this step, produces an installer that refuses to run.

## After installing

```bash
asd --update
```
Getting Started.Configuration:
| Variable | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ANDROID_HOME` | `~/dev/Android/Sdk` | Android SDK root directory. |
| `ASD_CSV` | `~/.cache/asd/myket.csv` | Path to the local CSV package registry. |
| `ASD_CONNECTIONS` | `16` | Parallel download connections for multi-connection downloads. |
| `ASD_SKIP_CHECKSUM` | unset | Set to `1` to always skip SHA-1 checksum verification. |

`HOME` (or `USERPROFILE` on Windows) resolves the defaults above.

## Avoiding sudo

```bash
export ASD_CSV=~/.local/share/asd/myket.csv
export ANDROID_HOME=~/.local/share/android-sdk
asd --update
```

See [Sudo Handling](/asd/2.0.0/sudo-handling/) for when elevation triggers.

Guides.Downloads: caching and speed:
**This page describes 2.0.0's download engine, which is simpler than 3.0.0's** — most notably, 2.0.0 has **no resume support**. An interrupted download restarts from byte zero on the next attempt.

## Single-connection downloads

For small files, files under 1 MiB, or servers that don't support ranged requests, `asd` does a single, non-resumable `GET`. If the connection drops mid-transfer, the partial file is left in the system temp directory (2.0.0 downloads into a fresh `Directory.systemTemp.createTemp('asd_')` per install, not a persistent cache next to the registry) and the *next* attempt starts over completely.

## Multi-connection downloads

For files over 1 MiB where the server supports `Accept-Ranges: bytes`, the file is split into `ASD_CONNECTIONS` (default 16) equal byte-range chunks downloaded in parallel to `.partN` files, then concatenated. If any single chunk's request fails, the **entire download fails** — there's no per-chunk retry or resume in 2.0.0; that was added in 3.0.0.

## Progress

A basic single-line progress indicator (`Downloading... 42.3% (128.4MB / 303.9MB)`, no speed or ETA) is printed roughly every 200ms. Live throughput and ETA estimates were added in 3.0.0.

## No download cache

Because archives are downloaded to a temp directory that's deleted after each install, `--fix` and `--verify` cannot reuse a previously-downloaded archive — every checksum re-verification always re-downloads. The persistent `downloads/` cache next to the CSV registry (which enables resume and archive reuse) was introduced in 3.0.0.
Guides.Repairing Installations:
## `asd --fix`

In 2.0.0, `--fix` performs a single check: for every installed package (or the one matching a given filter), it counts files under the install directory other than `package.xml`. If that count is zero, the directory is deleted and the package is reinstalled from scratch.

```bash
asd --fix        # check and repair everything installed
asd --fix ndk    # check and repair only packages matching "ndk"
```

This is meaningfully less thorough than 3.0.0's `--fix`: 2.0.0 does **not** check whether `package.xml` itself is parseable, does **not** check whether the package still exists in the registry (an orphaned package with content files would be reported "OK" even if it's no longer installable), and does **not** check the cached archive's checksum, since there is no persistent archive cache in this version. Those checks — and the distinct issue categories (`missingXml`, `notInRegistry`, `checksumMismatch`) — were added in 3.0.0.

## `asd --verify`

Behaves the same as in later versions at the command level: re-downloads the archive for an installed package and compares its SHA-1 against the registry. In 2.0.0 this download is always a fresh download to a temp file (no cache reuse), since the persistent `downloads/` cache doesn't exist yet.

```bash
asd --verify ndk 27.0.12077973
```
Guides.Sudo Handling:
Identical behavior to 3.0.0: every operation is attempted as the current user first, and only re-launched with `sudo` (Linux/macOS only) on a `FileSystemException` matching a permission error code. Windows prints a message to re-run from an elevated terminal instead of retrying automatically.

```bash
export ASD_CSV=~/.local/share/asd/myket.csv
export ANDROID_HOME=~/.local/share/android-sdk
asd --update
```

This subsystem hasn't changed since 1.0.0.

API Reference.Differences from 1.0.0:
`bin/asd.dart` is functionally unchanged between 1.0.0 and 2.0.0 (a single one-line diff removing an unnecessary `const` on a `ZLibDecoder` constructor call — no behavioral change). Everything below is new or changed in 2.0.0:

- **Offline installer embedding** (`tool/embed_installer.dart`, and the corresponding rewrite of `bin/installer.dart` to decode a baked-in payload instead of copying a neighboring binary file). See [Installer & Embedding](/asd/2.0.0/installer-embedding/).
- **CI** now builds and publishes the installer for both platforms as part of the release, alongside the `asd` binary itself.
- **README** was added in this release (1.0.0 shipped without one).

Everything else — the CLI dispatch, all 7 flags, the CSV registry format and matching logic, the download engine (including its lack of resume support), the SHA-1 implementation, the ZIP extraction engine (including its lack of Unix-permission/symlink preservation), `package.xml` handling, and `--fix`'s file-count-only diagnosis — is identical to 1.0.0.

Project.Overview:
`asd` 2.0.0 is released under the MIT License.

## What's new in 2.0.0

The offline, self-contained installer — see [Installer & Embedding](/asd/2.0.0/installer-embedding/). This is the sole feature addition over 1.0.0; the core `asd` tool itself is otherwise unchanged.

## What's next

3.0.0 substantially reworks the download engine (resume support, per-chunk retry, a persistent cache) and the ZIP extractor (Unix permissions, symlinks, ZIP64 support for large archives), and makes `--fix` diagnose several distinct failure modes instead of just "empty directory." See the [3.0.0 docs](/asd/installation/) for the current release.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
`asd` (Android SDK Downloader) is a single-file, dependency-free Dart CLI that downloads Android SDK components directly from the [Myket](https://myket.ir) mirror (`maven.myket.ir`), as an alternative to Google's `sdkmanager`.

This is the **1.0.0** release — the first published version. It shipped without a README; the documentation on this page is reconstructed from the source and CLI help text.

## Install

1.0.0's installer is a **two-file** installer: it expects an `asd` (or `asd.exe`) binary to already be sitting next to the `installer` executable — typically because both were extracted from the same release archive — and copies it into place. See [Installation](/asd/1.0.0/installation/).

## Fetch the package registry

```bash
asd --update
```

## Install something

```bash
asd platform-tools
asd ndk
asd build-tools 34.0.0
```

See [Commands](/asd/1.0.0/commands/) for the full reference.

## Requirements

- Dart SDK `>=3.0.0 <4.0.0` (to build from source only).
- Linux or Windows.
Getting Started.Installation:
1.0.0's installer does **not** embed the `asd` binary inside itself — that came in 2.0.0. Instead, it looks for a binary named `asd` (or `asd.exe` on Windows) in the same directory as its own executable, and copies that file into the install location.

```bash
# both installer-linux and asd-linux must be in the same directory
chmod +x installer-linux asd-linux
mv asd-linux asd
./installer-linux                 # installs to /usr/local/bin
./installer-linux ~/.local/bin    # or a directory you already own
```

If `asd` isn't found next to the installer, it fails immediately:

```
Error: Could not find 'asd' next to this installer at <path>. Make sure the
installer and the asd binary were extracted from the same release archive.
```

## Manual

Download the `asd` binary from Releases, rename it if necessary, and place it on your `PATH` directly — this always worked the same way regardless of installer version.

## Building from source

```bash
dart pub get
dart compile exe bin/asd.dart -o asd
dart compile exe bin/installer.dart -o installer
```

No embedding step exists yet in 1.0.0 — `tool/embed_installer.dart` was introduced in 2.0.0. Compiling `bin/installer.dart` directly is the normal (only) way to build it in this version.

Guides.Downloads: caching and speed:
1.0.0's download engine has no resume support and no persistent cache — both were added in 3.0.0.

## Single-connection downloads

Used for small files, files under 1 MiB, or when the server doesn't support ranged requests. A single non-resumable `GET` streams directly to a temp file. Any connection failure fails the whole download with no retry.

## Multi-connection downloads

For files over 1 MiB with range support, the file is split into up to `ASD_CONNECTIONS` (default **8** in this version) parallel chunks, each written to its own `.partN` file, then concatenated. As in 2.0.0, a single failed chunk fails the entire download — no per-chunk retry.

## Progress

A single-line percentage/byte-count indicator, printed on a timer (no speed or ETA — those were added in 3.0.0).

## No cache

Archives download to a fresh, randomly-named temp directory (`Directory.systemTemp.createTemp('asd_')`) that's deleted immediately after each install (successful or not), so nothing is reused by later commands.
Guides.Repairing Installations:
## `asd --fix`

Checks every installed package's directory for the presence of any file other than `package.xml`. An empty directory (zero content files) is deleted and reinstalled from scratch. This is the only check `--fix` performs in this version — checking `package.xml`'s own integrity, cross-referencing the registry, and verifying cached-archive checksums were all added later (3.0.0).

```bash
asd --fix
asd --fix ndk
```

## `asd --verify`

Re-downloads the installed package's archive to a temp file and compares its SHA-1 against the registry's checksum column.

```bash
asd --verify ndk 27.0.12077973
```
Guides.Sudo Handling:
Same as in every later version: operations are attempted as the current user first, and only re-launched with `sudo` (Linux/macOS) if a `FileSystemException` reports a permission error. Windows tells you to re-run from an elevated terminal instead.

```bash
export ASD_CSV=~/.local/share/asd/myket.csv
export ANDROID_HOME=~/.local/share/android-sdk
asd --update
```

Project.Overview:
`asd` 1.0.0 is the first published release, under the MIT License. It shipped without a README.

## Known limitations at this version

- No download resume — an interrupted download restarts from zero.
- No per-chunk retry on multi-connection downloads — one failed chunk fails the whole download.
- `--fix` only detects empty install directories, not unreadable metadata, orphaned packages, or checksum drift.
- The installer requires the `asd` binary to be physically present next to it (no embedding).
- ZIP extraction doesn't preserve Unix executable permissions or symlinks, which can leave some SDK components (particularly NDK toolchains) not immediately runnable without a manual `chmod`.

All of these were addressed in later releases — see the [2.0.0](/asd/2.0.0/installation/) and current [3.0.0](/asd/installation/) docs.
